title: Communicative English for Academic Analysis in Biology
reference: Naresuan University, course 258201, semester 1/2569. Course plan pp. 8–12. Assessment plan p. 14. The syllabus groups weeks 4–5, 10–11 and 12–13. Their separate weekly tasks below are suggested teaching choices.

weeks.guide: Show students where to find your course rules. Ask them to use the AI disclosure format accepted by their lecturer.

slides.title: Whose words are these?
body: Practice source A, class reading: “Two birds nested in the old mango tree.”
Nok writes the same sentence in her report. What choices could she make to show where it came from?

slides.title: Show where the idea came from
body: Example: The class reading describes a mango tree with two nesting birds (Source A).
A paraphrase uses your wording. Keep the details accurate and name the source. Use quotation marks for copied words.

slides.title: Write and check
body: Write your own version of the reading. Exchange papers and underline the source credit.
If you used an allowed AI tool, describe its job and your check. Example: “I used AI to check verb tense. I checked the numbers myself.”
Exit: give one way to show which work is yours.

weeks.topic: Article structure, database searching and pretest
weeks.guide: Use the approved pretest before practice (5% in the assessment plan). Pair chapter 02 with chapter 03 for the database workshop. Use the two fictional practice records on the slides for offline practice.

slides.title: Find the job of each section
body: Introduction asks a question. Methods tell how it was studied. Results report findings. Discussion explains what they might mean.
“We counted frogs on two paths” describes Methods. “We saw 12 frogs” reports Results.

slides.title: Search for a biology article
body: Question: How does shade affect leaf size? Try “shade AND leaf size” in a scientific database. Use OR to include a second term, such as shade OR shading.
Compare the two classroom records on the next slide. Which one would you open first for original data?

slides.title: Compare two practice records
body: Record A · Leaf width on two paths. An EDOS class measured ten leaves on each path. The means were 6 cm and 4 cm.
Record B · Reading about leaves and light. An EDOS group compared three reports and collected no new measurements.
Both records are fictional and are supplied for class practice.

slides.title: Choose a useful source
body: Which record reports measurements of leaf size? Which is a review of past studies? Point to the words that helped you decide.
Trade choices. Give one reason the source fits your question and one detail you still need to check.

weeks.guide: Ask students to skim silently, then scan for one detail and close-read a limitation. Transfer the same three steps to a supplied article abstract.

slides.title: Read a short abstract
body: Practice text: “We asked where snails rest on campus. On one wet morning, we checked ten trees. We found more snails near the ground than above eye level.”

slides.title: Read it three ways
body: Skim for the purpose: Where do snails rest?
Scan for a detail: How many trees were checked?
Read closely: Which words limit the time of the observation?

slides.title: Make a reading log
body: Try a second text: “We asked whether leaf width differed on two paths. On one morning, we measured ten leaves per path. Their mean widths were 6 cm and 4 cm.” Write its question, one exact detail and one limit.
Swap logs. Your partner should be able to point to each answer in the text.

weeks.guide: First part of the shared weeks 4–5 topic. Use a short sentence before students work with an article paragraph.

slides.title: Keep the meaning
body: Source A, practice passage: “On this visit, bees landed on yellow flowers more often than on white flowers.”
Possible paraphrase: During the visit, white flowers received fewer bee visits than yellow ones (Source A).

slides.title: Try a new sentence
body: Source B: “Six of the ten nests were under the roof.”
Read, cover the sentence, and tell a partner what it means. Then write it in a new sentence and credit Source B.

slides.title: Check the boundaries
body: Compare your answer with Source B. Keep the numbers, location and meaning.
Would “Most birds build nests under roofs” keep the same meaning? Explain your choice.

weeks.guide: Second part of the shared weeks 4–5 topic. For peer feedback, ask students to point to the main idea and one detail they chose to leave out.

slides.title: Find the core idea
body: Practice passage: “A class watched a pond for ten minutes. Students saw five frogs at the edge and one on a rock. The rock was smooth and grey. Most frogs they saw stayed near the edge.”

slides.title: Choose details for your reader
body: For a reader asking where the frogs were, the place matters. The colour of the rock can be left out.
One summary: During a short pond visit, the class saw most frogs near the edge.

slides.title: Summarize another paragraph
body: Use a paragraph from the assigned article. Write one sentence with its main idea. Add one important detail if needed. Name the source.
Trade summaries. Does each one keep the original claim and its limits?

weeks.guide: Use two short introductions. Students identify what is known, the gap, the aim and how each author gathered evidence. Show chapter 02 for section names.

slides.title: Find the gap
body: Practice introduction: “We know which birds visit this garden in the morning. We have little information about afternoon visits. We asked whether the visitor counts differ.”
Gap: afternoon visits. Aim: compare morning and afternoon counts.

slides.title: Separate prediction and method
body: Prediction: “We expected more visits in the morning.” Method: “We counted visits for ten minutes at each time.”
Which sentence says what the writers expected? Which tells readers what they did?

slides.title: Read a second example
body: “Students often count butterflies on sunny days. Counts on cloudy days are missing. We watched the same garden on two cloudy days.”
State the gap. Suggest an aim. Use “may” to give one reason the short study has limited evidence.

weeks.guide: Teach the difference between a measured result and an interpretation. Use the prepared catalase table activity in chapter 06 for further practice.

slides.title: Read two counts
body: Practice data from one ten-minute count per site: garden, 8 birds; field, 4 birds.
Results: “We counted four more birds in the garden than in the field.” Which words report the comparison?

slides.title: Discuss the result carefully
body: Discussion: “The garden may have attracted more birds during this visit.”
Why would we need more visits to say where birds are usually found?

slides.title: Write from a fresh table
body: Use the chapter table. Write one Results sentence with two values and a unit. Then write one Discussion sentence about what the data suggest.
Ask a partner to underline the numbers and circle the word that shows caution.

weeks.guide: Midterm assessment (15%). The syllabus specifies article structure, a summary and interpretation of a figure or table. Use a lecturer-selected assessment article. The following example is for preparation.

slides.title: Practice the reading sequence
body: Practice extract: “We counted flowers in two plots. Plot A had 11 open flowers. Plot B had 7.”
The first sentence describes a method. The next two report a result. Summarize the finding in your own words.

slides.title: Interpret a table
body: Practice counts of open flowers: plot C, 9; plot D, 12. Write one comparison with the correct unit.
Possible response: Plot D had three more open flowers than plot C. Check your subtraction and the group names.

slides.title: Before you submit
body: Check the labels you gave the article sections. Read your summary alongside the text. Match each number to its group and unit.

weeks.guide: Use the same findings twice. Students first write a conclusion, then place it in a short structured and unstructured abstract.

slides.title: What does a conclusion do?
body: Practice notes: Question—where did we see more snails? Method—one ten-minute count per path. Findings—shaded path, 9; open path, 3.
Conclusion: On this visit we saw more snails on the shaded path. More visits could test whether this pattern repeats.

slides.title: Build a short abstract
body: Aim: We compared snail counts on two paths. Method: We counted each path for ten minutes.
Result: We saw nine snails on the shaded path and three on the open path. Conclusion: Counts differed on this visit.

slides.title: Change the format
body: Write the four ideas under the headings Aim, Methods, Results and Conclusion.
Now write them as one short paragraph without headings. Ask a partner to find all four ideas.

weeks.guide: First part of the shared weeks 10–11 topic. Have each student plan an introduction, a body paragraph and a conclusion before drafting.

slides.title: Choose a claim you can support
body: Practice note: At midday on one day, students saw 4 bees by plot A and 10 by plot B.
Possible claim: Plot B had more bee visits in this count. Which words keep the claim close to the evidence?

slides.title: Plan three parts
body: Introduction: give the question and your claim. Body: compare the counts and explain what the comparison tells us. Conclusion: return to the claim and give one limit.

slides.title: Make your own plan
body: Use the result section of an assigned article. Write one line for each part.
Read your body plan aloud. Can your partner tell which evidence supports your claim?

weeks.guide: Second part of the shared weeks 10–11 topic. Ask students to highlight evidence and analysis in different ways, then revise one transition.

slides.title: Give each sentence a job
body: Practice paragraph: “The counts differed by site. We saw ten bees in plot B and four in plot A. This difference suggests that visits were uneven that day. However, one visit tells us little about other days.”

slides.title: Trace the argument
body: Which sentence states the topic? Which reports evidence? Which explains it?
“However” introduces a limit. Try reading the paragraph with “therefore” instead. What changes?

slides.title: Revise a paragraph
body: Underline a number or observation in your draft. Write a sentence explaining how it supports your claim. Add a transition to the next idea.
Exchange drafts. Ask your partner to point to the evidence, explanation and transition.

weeks.guide: First part of the shared weeks 12–13 topic. Use short extracts and a comparison table with one row per source.

slides.title: Make a comparison table
body: Practice study A: Observers counted 12 birds in a garden and 4 in a field for ten minutes each.
Practice study B: Observers counted 9 birds in a garden and 6 in a field for five minutes each.

slides.title: Compare the pattern
body: Each study found more birds in its garden count. Their counting times differed.
Record the place, count time and direction of the difference for each study.

slides.title: Explain one limit
body: Can you compare the two raw garden counts as if the observation times were equal? Explain.
Share one point of agreement and one difference in how the two studies gathered evidence.

weeks.guide: Second part of the shared weeks 12–13 topic. Students turn a comparison table into one paragraph linking both sources. The chapter 07 activity provides a longer task.

slides.title: Connect two sources
body: Practice A: A garden count found more birds near trees than near a wall. Practice B: A second garden count found similar numbers at both places.

slides.title: Show agreement or difference
body: Possible opening: “Both studies compared birds in two places, but only study A found more birds near trees.”
The two results can both be accurate. What extra detail would help you compare the studies?

slides.title: Write and review
body: Use two assigned sources. Write their shared question, one finding from each, and what the evidence supports together. Name both sources.
Check that your final sentence connects the sources. Ask a partner to explain the link.

weeks.guide: Run a short Q&A roleplay. Partners should listen for a clear claim, a question about evidence and a polite answer.

slides.title: Disagree politely
body: A: “The garden always has more birds.” B: “I see why you think so. Could one short visit show what happens every day?”
A: “You are right about the time. I can say we saw more birds there on this visit.”

slides.title: Use the language
body: To ask for evidence: “Which part of the table supports that?” To be cautious: “This may mean …” To clarify: “Do you mean …?”

slides.title: Take turns
body: Use a chapter table. A makes a claim. B asks for evidence or a limit. A answers with a value or a detail. Switch roles.
Exit: give one phrase that helped your partner stay in the discussion.

weeks.guide: Use the syllabus two-minute mock presentation. Ask the listener to identify the research question and one result without looking at the notes.

slides.title: Guide your listener
body: Opening: “Today I will explain one finding from this article.” Evidence: “Look at the two bars.” Closing: “On this visit, the counts differed.”

slides.title: Build one clear visual
body: Practice counts: garden, 8 birds; field, 4 birds. Draw two labelled bars. Name the unit and give the chart a question as its title.
Point to one bar while saying its value. Pause before you compare it with the other bar.

slides.title: Rehearse a short talk
body: Choose one result from your article. Speak for two minutes using a question, a visual and a closing sentence.
Partner: repeat the main finding and suggest one signpost that could make the talk easier to follow.

weeks.topic: Group oral presentation and course reflection
weeks.guide: The syllabus calls for an 8–10 minute group presentation on a selected article, Q&A and reflection. Oral presentation is 10% and peer assessment is 5% in the published assessment plan. Use the lecturer’s approved rubric.

slides.title: Prepare the group handover
body: Each speaker introduces one part of the same article analysis. Example handover: “Mali has shown the result. I will explain one limit.”
Agree on who will display the figure and who will take the first question.

slides.title: Present and listen
body: Groups: present the article analysis in about 8–10 minutes. Use evidence and credit your source. Then take questions.
Listeners: note one claim, one supporting detail and one question. Give feedback using the course rubric.

slides.title: Reflect after speaking
body: Finish these sentences: “I explained ___ clearly when I ___.” “Next time I will practise ___ by ___.”
Choose one activity from the course to help with your next step.

weeks.guide: Final assessment (15%). The syllabus requires an unseen article, an analytical essay, and analysis of structure and content. Select a fresh article under the course exam arrangements. These slides provide practice only.

slides.title: Rehearse a short analysis
body: Practice extract: “We compared bird counts near trees and near a wall. In one visit, we counted nine birds near trees and three near the wall.”
What was the aim? Which sentence gives evidence? What limit can you identify?

slides.title: Build the essay from evidence
body: Example point: The counts support a difference on the day observed. They come from one visit.
Plan an introduction, a body paragraph that uses evidence from the article, and a conclusion with a limit.

slides.title: Check your response
body: Does your essay answer the question? Can a reader trace each claim to the article?
Check the section labels, values and units. Leave time to read your ending once.
